findings.claim: Of 9,898 moves in 469 games that reached a position with at most 5 pieces, 160 were tablebase errors: 72 by the player and 88 by the opponents.
findings.metric: count of tablebase errors (moves that change the Syzygy result from the mover's view) in positions with at most 5 pieces
findings.caveat: Only 9,898 moves in 469 games reach tablebase range, and only 160 of them are errors; every material or clock cell is small.

findings.section: 1. Did you convert tablebase wins and hold tablebase draws?
findings.claim: The player converted tablebase-won endings into wins on the scoreboard slightly more often than opponents converted theirs, with a CI that includes zero.
findings.metric: share of games whose first <=5-piece position was a tablebase win for the side that ended as a win on the scoreboard; player's games vs games where the opponent had the tablebase win
findings.n: 210 player tablebase wins, 198 opponent tablebase wins
findings.caveat: Game-level conversion compares different games for the player and the opponents; the difference CI treats them as independent samples. Opponents are rating-matched (within about 27 points) but are many different people.

findings.section: 1. Did you convert tablebase wins and hold tablebase draws?
findings.claim: In bullet the player converted tablebase-won endings 63% of the time, no better than opponents.
findings.metric: share of tablebase-won endings (first <=5-piece position) that ended as a win on the scoreboard
findings.n: 93 player tablebase wins, 89 opponent tablebase wins
findings.caveat: Different games for each side; the difference CI treats them as independent samples.

findings.section: 1. Did you convert tablebase wins and hold tablebase draws?
findings.claim: In blitz the player converted tablebase-won endings more often than opponents, with a CI that includes zero.
findings.metric: share of tablebase-won endings (first <=5-piece position) that ended as a win on the scoreboard
findings.n: 92 player tablebase wins, 92 opponent tablebase wins
findings.caveat: Different games for each side; the difference CI treats them as independent samples.

findings.section: 1. Did you convert tablebase wins and hold tablebase draws?
findings.claim: In rapid the player converted tablebase-won endings more often than opponents, on a small sample with a CI that includes zero.
findings.metric: share of tablebase-won endings (first <=5-piece position) that ended as a win on the scoreboard
findings.n: 25 player tablebase wins, 17 opponent tablebase wins
findings.caveat: Small sample; different games for each side.

findings.section: 1. Did you convert tablebase wins and hold tablebase draws?
findings.claim: The player held tablebase-drawn endings (did not lose them) less often than opponents held the same drawn endings.
findings.metric: share of games whose first <=5-piece position was a tablebase draw that did not end as a loss for the side
findings.caveat: Hold rates use the same drawn games for both sides (a draw the player failed to hold is a draw they converted), so they are not independent of each other.

findings.section: 1. Did you convert tablebase wins and hold tablebase draws?
findings.claim: In bullet the player held tablebase-drawn endings far less often than opponents held the same drawn endings, on 16 games.
findings.metric: share of tablebase-drawn endings (first <=5-piece position) that did not end as a loss for the side
findings.caveat: Same drawn games for both sides, so the two rates are not independent; very small cell.

findings.section: 1. Did you convert tablebase wins and hold tablebase draws?
findings.claim: In blitz the player and opponents held tablebase-drawn endings at the same rate.
findings.metric: share of tablebase-drawn endings (first <=5-piece position) that did not end as a loss for the side
findings.caveat: Same drawn games for both sides, so the two rates are not independent.

findings.section: 1. Did you convert tablebase wins and hold tablebase draws?
findings.claim: In rapid every tablebase-drawn ending was held by both sides.
findings.metric: share of tablebase-drawn endings (first <=5-piece position) that did not end as a loss for the side
findings.caveat: Nine games only.

findings.section: What this means for the player
findings.claim: Of the player's 51 failed conversions, 33 ended by timeout or 'timeout vs insufficient material' without any tablebase error, 29 of them in bullet.
findings.metric: count of the player's tablebase-won endings that ended drawn or lost by timeout or timeout vs insufficient material with no tablebase error by the player
findings.n: 51 failed conversions by the player (55 by the opponents)
findings.caveat: Repetition, 50-move and agreed draws without any tablebase error are counted as failed conversions by the rules, not as technique errors.

findings.section: How the failed conversions and failed holds ended
findings.claim: The player's tablebase wins ended as draws by 'timeout vs insufficient material' with no tablebase error more often than the opponents' did (23 vs 15 games), almost all in bullet (21 vs 14).
findings.metric: count of tablebase-won endings that ended by the chess.com timeout-vs-insufficient-material draw with no tablebase error by the winning side
findings.n: 51 failed conversions by the player, 55 by the opponents
findings.caveat: Raw counts without CIs.

findings.section: How the failed conversions and failed holds ended
findings.claim: The player's tablebase wins were lost on time with no tablebase error in 10 games against 4 for the opponents.
findings.metric: count of tablebase-won endings that ended by timeout with no tablebase error by the winning side
findings.n: 51 failed conversions by the player, 55 by the opponents
findings.caveat: Raw counts without CIs.

findings.section: How the failed conversions and failed holds ended
findings.claim: Fewer of the player's failed conversions involved a tablebase error by the winner than the opponents' did (18 vs 33 games).
findings.metric: count of tablebase-won endings not converted where the winning side made at least one tablebase error
findings.n: 51 failed conversions by the player, 55 by the opponents
findings.caveat: Raw counts without CIs.

findings.section: How the failed conversions and failed holds ended
findings.claim: 35 of the player's tablebase wins ended lost or drawn on the clock (with or without an earlier tablebase error), against 21 of the opponents'.
findings.metric: count of tablebase-won endings that ended drawn or lost by timeout or timeout vs insufficient material, with or without an earlier tablebase error
findings.n: 210 player tablebase wins, 198 opponent tablebase wins
findings.caveat: Raw counts without CIs.

findings.claim: In positions with at most 5 pieces the player threw away a win or a draw on fewer moves per 100 than opponents, with overlapping CIs.
findings.metric: tablebase errors (win->draw/loss or draw->loss) per 100 moves played from won or drawn positions
findings.caveat: Only 160 errors in total; CIs overlap.

findings.claim: In bullet the tablebase error rate per 100 at-risk moves was similar for the player and opponents.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves played from won or drawn positions
findings.caveat: Small cells; CIs overlap.

findings.claim: In blitz the tablebase error rate per 100 at-risk moves was slightly lower for the player than for opponents.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves played from won or drawn positions
findings.caveat: CIs overlap.

findings.claim: In rapid the tablebase error rate per 100 at-risk moves was similar for the player and opponents.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves played from won or drawn positions
findings.caveat: Small cells; CIs overlap.

findings.claim: The player spoiled tablebase-won positions into draws on half as many moves per 100 as opponents did.
findings.metric: win->draw tablebase errors per 100 moves played from won positions
findings.caveat: The tablebase columns hold only win/draw/loss (no cursed-win distinction for the 50-move rule).

findings.claim: Turning a tablebase win straight into a loss was rare for both sides.
findings.metric: win->loss tablebase errors per 100 moves played from won positions
findings.caveat: Two and three events only.

findings.claim: The player lost tablebase-drawn positions on more moves per 100 than opponents did, mostly in pawn and rook endings.
findings.metric: draw->loss tablebase errors per 100 moves played from drawn positions
findings.caveat: CIs overlap; only 529 drawn-position moves by the player.

findings.claim: Inside tablebase range in bullet, calibrated expected points lost per move were the same for the player and opponents.
findings.metric: mean ep_loss per move in positions with at most 5 pieces, all positions, both sides
findings.caveat: cp_loss gives the same picture: 25.1 [17.5, 34.2] vs 27.7 [19.9, 35.7].

findings.claim: Inside tablebase range in blitz, the player lost fewer calibrated expected points per move than opponents, with a CI that excludes zero.
findings.metric: mean ep_loss per move in positions with at most 5 pieces, all positions, both sides

findings.claim: Inside tablebase range in rapid, calibrated expected points lost per move were the same for the player and opponents.
findings.metric: mean ep_loss per move in positions with at most 5 pieces, all positions, both sides
findings.caveat: 51 games only.

findings.claim: Rook endings (rook and pawns vs rook and pawns) are the material class with the highest tablebase error rate for both sides, at about 13 errors per 100 at-risk moves.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won-or-drawn positions, rook ending material class
findings.caveat: Driven by rook and pawn versus rook from either side (KRvKRP: 13 / 54 player errors, 16 / 60 opponents; KRPvKR: 12 / 114 vs 10 / 81); small cells.

findings.claim: In pawn endings the player and opponents made tablebase errors at similar rates.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won-or-drawn positions, pawn ending material class
findings.caveat: CIs overlap.

findings.claim: With a queen against pawns or a bare king, the player made fewer tablebase errors per 100 moves than opponents.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won-or-drawn positions, queen vs pawns/bare king material class
findings.caveat: Few errors in absolute terms (7 vs 19).

findings.claim: With a rook against pawns or a bare king, both sides almost never made a tablebase error.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won-or-drawn positions, rook vs pawns/bare king material class
findings.caveat: Few errors in absolute terms.

findings.claim: When winning a pawn ending the player spoiled the win on fewer moves per 100 than opponents did.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won positions, pawn ending material class, winning side
findings.caveat: Small cells.

findings.claim: When winning a rook ending both sides spoiled the win on about one move in five from won positions.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won positions, rook ending material class, winning side
findings.caveat: Small cells with wide CIs.

findings.claim: When winning with a queen against pawns or a bare king the player spoiled the win on fewer moves per 100 than opponents did.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won positions, queen vs pawns/bare king material class, winning side
findings.caveat: Few errors in absolute terms (6 vs 18).

findings.claim: When defending a drawn pawn ending the player lost it on more moves per 100 than opponents did.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from drawn positions, pawn ending material class, defending side
findings.caveat: Small cells; CIs nearly touch.

findings.claim: When defending a drawn rook ending both sides lost it on about one move in ten from drawn positions.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from drawn positions, rook ending material class, defending side
findings.caveat: Small cells.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: With under 5 seconds on the clock the player's tablebase error rate was no higher than with 60 seconds or more.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won-or-drawn positions, mover's clock before the move under 5 s, all time classes pooled
findings.caveat: Tablebase positions arrive late in the game, so clock effects are confounded with the time class and with how long the game has lasted.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: With 5-15 seconds on the clock the tablebase error rate was the highest of the clock bands for both sides.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won-or-drawn positions, mover's clock before the move 5-15 s, all time classes pooled
findings.caveat: Clock effects are confounded with the time class and game length; all clock-band CIs overlap.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: With 15-60 seconds on the clock the player's tablebase error rate was slightly above the opponents'.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won-or-drawn positions, mover's clock before the move 15-60 s, all time classes pooled
findings.caveat: Clock effects are confounded with the time class and game length; CIs overlap.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: With 60 seconds or more on the clock the player made fewer tablebase errors per 100 moves than opponents.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won-or-drawn positions, mover's clock before the move >= 60 s, all time classes pooled
findings.caveat: Clock effects are confounded with the time class and game length.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: In blitz with under 15 seconds left, both sides made more tablebase errors per 100 moves than with 15 seconds or more, the player less so than opponents.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won-or-drawn positions, blitz, mover's clock before the move under 15 s
findings.caveat: Baseline at >= 15 s is 2.4 [1.3, 3.6] (player) vs 3.0 [1.8, 4.2] (opponents); small cells, CIs overlap.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: In bullet with under 15 seconds left the tablebase error rate was not higher than with 15 seconds or more, for either side.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won-or-drawn positions, bullet, mover's clock before the move under 15 s
findings.caveat: Baseline at >= 15 s is 2.8 [0.6, 5.7] (player) vs 3.4 [1.1, 6.7] (opponents); most bullet tablebase moves are under 15 s.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: In won positions one or two moves from a winning capture or pawn move (DTZ 1-2) the player spoiled the win on fewer moves per 100 than opponents.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won positions with Syzygy DTZ 1-2
findings.caveat: DTZ is from the side to move and binned coarsely.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: Won positions 3-5 moves from a winning capture or pawn move (DTZ 3-5) had the highest error rate of any DTZ band for both sides.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won positions with Syzygy DTZ 3-5
findings.caveat: Baseline at DTZ 1-2 is 0.7 [0.3, 1.3] (player) vs 1.9 [1.1, 2.9] (opponents); DTZ is binned coarsely.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: In won positions with DTZ 6-10 the player spoiled the win on fewer moves per 100 than opponents.
findings.metric: tablebase errors per 100 moves from won positions with Syzygy DTZ 6-10
findings.caveat: Three errors by the player; small cells.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: On won-position moves with DTZ 3-5 the player spent less time per move than opponents did.
findings.metric: mean seconds spent on the move, won positions with Syzygy DTZ 3-5
findings.caveat: Time spent per move is from the clock comments and undercounts lag and pre-move time; time classes pooled.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: While winning in tablebase range in bullet the player spent the same time per move as opponents but a larger share of the remaining clock.
findings.metric: mean seconds spent per move while the mover has a tablebase win, positions with at most 5 pieces
findings.caveat: Share of remaining clock per move: 0.129 [0.112, 0.148] (player) vs 0.099 [0.081, 0.116] (opponents); time spent undercounts lag and pre-move time.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: While winning in tablebase range in bullet the player used a larger share of the remaining clock per move than opponents, i.e. was lower on the clock for the same seconds spent.
findings.metric: mean share of the mover's remaining clock spent on the move while the mover has a tablebase win, positions with at most 5 pieces
findings.caveat: Time spent per move is from the clock comments and undercounts lag and pre-move time.

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: While winning in tablebase range in blitz the player spent less time per move than opponents.
findings.metric: mean seconds spent per move while the mover has a tablebase win, positions with at most 5 pieces
findings.caveat: Share of remaining clock is the same for both sides: 0.060 [0.050, 0.070] vs 0.057 [0.046, 0.070].

findings.section: 4. Clock, distance to conversion, and time spent
findings.claim: While winning in tablebase range in rapid the player spent less time per move than opponents.
findings.metric: mean seconds spent per move while the mover has a tablebase win, positions with at most 5 pieces
findings.caveat: Share of remaining clock: 0.020 [0.011, 0.032] (player) vs 0.012 [0.009, 0.016] (opponents); 45 games.

findings.claim: In bullet endgames with rook and minor pieces (more than 5 pieces) the player lost slightly fewer calibrated expected points per move than opponents, with a CI that excludes zero.
findings.metric: mean ep_loss per endgame-phase move with more than 5 pieces, rook + minor material class
findings.caveat: cp_loss points the other way (75 [72, 78] vs 74 [71, 77]); material classes are coarse (piece types present, regardless of which side has what).

findings.claim: In bullet endgames with a queen plus other pieces the player lost slightly fewer calibrated expected points per move than opponents, with a CI that excludes zero; this class has the highest ep_loss per move of any.
findings.metric: mean ep_loss per endgame-phase move with more than 5 pieces, queen + others material class
findings.caveat: cp_loss: 74 [69, 80] vs 72 [66, 77]; the endgame phase beyond 5 pieces is the material heuristic from the enrichment.

findings.claim: In bullet rook endings with more than 5 pieces, calibrated expected points lost per move were the same for the player and opponents.
findings.metric: mean ep_loss per endgame-phase move with more than 5 pieces, rook ending material class
findings.caveat: cp_loss is higher for the player here: 62 [58, 66] vs 58 [54, 62].

findings.claim: In blitz endgames with rook and minor pieces (more than 5 pieces) calibrated expected points lost per move were the same for the player and opponents.
findings.metric: mean ep_loss per endgame-phase move with more than 5 pieces, rook + minor material class
findings.caveat: Material classes are coarse (piece types present, regardless of which side has what).

findings.claim: In blitz rook endings with more than 5 pieces, calibrated expected points lost per move were the same for the player and opponents.
findings.metric: mean ep_loss per endgame-phase move with more than 5 pieces, rook ending material class

findings.claim: In rapid endgames with a queen plus other pieces the player lost fewer calibrated expected points per move than opponents, with a CI that just includes zero.
findings.metric: mean ep_loss per endgame-phase move with more than 5 pieces, queen + others material class
findings.caveat: cp_loss agrees in direction: 67 [55, 81] vs 80 [65, 95]; CI includes zero.

findings.claim: In rapid minor-piece endgames with more than 5 pieces the player lost fewer calibrated expected points per move than opponents, with a CI that includes zero.
findings.metric: mean ep_loss per endgame-phase move with more than 5 pieces, minor piece ending material class
findings.caveat: 33 games; CI includes zero.

findings.claim: In bullet endgame-phase positions with more than 5 pieces the player made a move losing at least 0.10 expected points slightly less often than opponents, with a CI that just excludes zero.
findings.metric: share of endgame-phase moves (> 5 pieces) with ep_loss >= 0.10
findings.caveat: The upper CI bound is -0.0, i.e. the difference is at the edge of significance.

findings.claim: In blitz endgame-phase positions with more than 5 pieces the player and opponents made moves losing at least 0.10 expected points equally often.
findings.metric: share of endgame-phase moves (> 5 pieces) with ep_loss >= 0.10

findings.claim: In rapid endgame-phase positions with more than 5 pieces the player made a move losing at least 0.10 expected points slightly less often than opponents, with a CI that includes zero.
findings.metric: share of endgame-phase moves (> 5 pieces) with ep_loss >= 0.10
findings.caveat: 284 games; CI includes zero.
